slides.title: Executive Reports Serve a Different Purpose Than Debriefs
bullets: A strategically important congress often needs a report for leadership
Aimed at Medical Affairs leadership, sometimes other leadership functions
It doesn't document everything: it synthesizes what leaders need to decide

slides.title: Lead With the Conclusion, Not the Timeline
bullets: Open with a one-page summary, not a day-by-day narrative
What changed in the scientific or competitive landscape?
What does it mean for the product's medical strategy?
What decisions or investments need attention soon?
What new risks or opportunities appeared?

slides.title: What Follows the Summary
bullets: Key scientific data presented, own and competitor, with strategic implications
The competitive landscape summarized by key messages, not detailed transcripts
The most significant insights, grouped by theme and prioritized by impact
The relationship or collaboration opportunities with the highest strategic relevance

slides.title: Two Mistakes That Undermine a Report
bullets: Detail overload: dozens of data points and anecdotes with no hierarchy
That dilutes the main message and wastes limited leadership attention
Missing implication: listing what happened without a recommendation
A good report always connects findings to a decision or a question

slides.title: Format Carries Part of the Message
bullets: Clear structure with headlines that state the conclusion first
Simple visual aids where they help synthesize complex information
A contained length that respects a leader's limited reading time
Executive communication skills are developed further later in the course

takeaway.title: An executive report earns leadership's attention by leading with what matters most
bullets: It synthesizes decisions, not a full record of what happened
Leading with the conclusion beats narrating the congress chronologically
Overload and missing implications are the two mistakes that undermine it
